prompt: On Android, which kind of permission does the person grant in a dialog while the app runs?

choices.text: Install-time, such as network access
choices.why: Install-time permissions are granted by the system when the app is installed.

choices.text: Signature permissions, between apps signed together
choices.why: Those are granted by matching certificates, not by the person.

choices.text: Runtime
choices.why: Right. Android also calls them dangerous permissions.

choices.text: Every permission declared in the manifest
choices.why: Declaring does not grant; only the runtime kind is asked for.

prompt: An iOS app calls the camera API without NSCameraUsageDescription in its Info.plist. What does Apple's documentation say happens?

choices.text: The system terminates the app
choices.why: Right. That is the media capture documentation's word, and App Review rejects such an app.

choices.text: The camera opens, and a warning is logged
choices.why: Access is not granted without the purpose string.

choices.text: The system shows a dialog with a default sentence
choices.why: There is no default sentence; the app supplies it or fails.

choices.text: The person is asked to type a reason
choices.why: The reason is the app's to write, not the person's.

prompt: Which of these does the planner need a permission for, on at least one platform? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: sending a reminder before a session
choices.why: Right: the notification permission, on both.

choices.text: reaching the network, on Android
choices.why: Right, though it is an install-time permission the person is never asked for.

choices.text: storing the plan on the device
choices.why: An app's own storage needs no permission.

choices.text: reading the student's contacts
choices.why: The planner does not need them, so it never asks.

prompt: A new app is installed on a phone with Android 13. Before it asks for anything, are its notifications on?

choices.text: Yes, until the person turns them off
choices.why: That was the old rule; from Android 13 they start off.

choices.text: Yes, as notifications are an install-time permission
choices.why: On Android 13 and later they are a runtime permission.

choices.text: Only those sent in the first week
choices.why: There is no grace week.

choices.text: No: they are off until POST_NOTIFICATIONS is granted
choices.why: Right, by Android's documentation on the notification permission.

prompt: On iOS, the sentence an app supplies to explain why it wants access is called the purpose ___.
On iOS, the person answers no to the notification dialog. The app asks again a week later. What happens?

choices.text: The dialog appears once more, as on Android
choices.why: That second chance is Android's, not iOS's.

choices.text: No dialog; the stored no comes back at once
choices.why: Right. Later calls do not prompt the person again.

choices.text: The dialog appears, with the app's rationale
choices.why: iOS has no rationale call and no second dialog.

choices.text: The system asks whether to reset the answer
choices.why: Nothing asks; only the person can change it in Settings.

prompt: On Android, when does shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() return true?

choices.text: Before the app has ever asked
choices.why: Before any ask it returns false.

choices.text: After one refusal, while one more dialog is still possible
choices.why: Right. It is the window in which to explain.

choices.text: After the denial has become permanent
choices.why: Then it returns false again.

choices.text: Whenever the permission is granted
choices.why: A granted permission needs no explanation.

prompt: An Android app sees shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() return false. Why can it not conclude that it has never asked?

choices.text: Because the call is unreliable on older phones
choices.why: The answer is reliable; it is the same answer for two different states.

choices.text: Because iOS shares the answer with Android
choices.why: The platforms share nothing here.

choices.text: Because false means the permission is granted
choices.why: Granted is checked with checkSelfPermission, not with this call.

choices.text: False also means refused for good
choices.why: Right. Not asked and permanently denied both return false, so the app has to remember whether it asked.

prompt: A person grants approximate location to an app that asked for precise. What should the app do?

choices.text: Work with what it was given
choices.why: Right, and ask for more only where a feature needs it. Android's documentation says the app should still work.

choices.text: Treat it as a refusal
choices.why: It is a yes, to part of the request.

choices.text: Ask again for precise at once
choices.why: That asks the person to undo the decision they just made.

choices.text: Close, since the feature is broken
choices.why: Nothing is broken; the location is less precise.

prompt: Match each partial yes to its platform's name for it.

pairs.left: a selection of photos, on iOS
a selection of photos, on Android 14

prompt: When should the planner ask for the notification permission?

choices.text: At the first launch, so that the question is out of the way
choices.why: The person has seen nothing yet, and a no there is costly.

choices.text: After the student has used it for a week
choices.why: A week is arbitrary; the moment is the feature, not the calendar.

choices.text: When the student taps "remind me"
choices.why: Right. The tap is the explanation.

choices.text: Each time it starts, until the answer is yes
choices.why: That is the nagging the documentation calls not respectful.

prompt: Why must the app's own explanation screen never look like the system's dialog?

choices.text: The person decides only in the real dialog
choices.why: Right, and an imitation is a trick. The app's screen explains and leads to the real one.

choices.text: Because the system draws over it and hides it
choices.why: The system does not hide an app's own screen.

choices.text: Because the stores charge a fee for custom dialogs
choices.why: No fee is involved.

choices.text: Because Kotlin cannot draw dialogs
choices.why: It draws dialogs; the point is honesty, not ability.

prompt: An app targets an Android version older than 13 and runs on an Android 13 phone. When does the notification dialog appear?

choices.text: Whenever the app calls launcher.launch
choices.why: That control belongs to apps targeting 13 or higher.

choices.text: Never; old apps keep notifications on
choices.why: On a new install they start off, and the system asks.

choices.text: When the system chooses, for most apps at start-up
choices.why: Right. Only an app targeting 13 or higher has complete control over the moment.

choices.text: Only after the first notification is lost
choices.why: The dialog does not wait for a loss.

prompt: The reminder permission was refused for good. Which of these should the planner do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: keep planning, marking and summing sessions
choices.why: Right. None of that needs the permission.

choices.text: say on the "remind me" button that reminders are off
choices.why: Right: be specific about the missing feature.

choices.text: offer a way to Settings when the student taps "remind me"
choices.why: Right: the only way back, at the moment it matters.

choices.text: show a full-screen warning at every launch
choices.why: The documentation says not to block the interface, and not to nag.

prompt: Put the planner's steps in order, for a student on Android who refused once before and taps "remind me" again.
items: check whether the permission is granted

prompt: In permission.ts, which line holds the whole difference between the platforms' no?

choices.text: export type State = ...
choices.why: The states are the same on both platforms.

choices.text: const final = p.platform === "ios" || p.state === "denied";
choices.why: Right. Any no on iOS, or a second no on Android, is final.

choices.text: if (p.state === "not-asked") return "ask when a reminder is wanted";
choices.why: That is what the planner does next, the same on both.

choices.text: export function fresh(platform)
choices.why: Every permission starts not asked, on both.

prompt: In the first Android table of ask.ts, how many system dialogs were shown to the student?
In the first Android table, why does the row "taps 'remind me'" show the dialog as none?

choices.text: The student had already granted it
choices.why: The state was denied-for-good.

choices.text: Because the planner forgot to ask
choices.why: It asked; the system answered without a dialog.

choices.text: Because notifications do not need a dialog
choices.why: On Android 13 and later they do.

choices.text: Two earlier refusals made it permanent
choices.why: Right. Both were spent at launch, before the student wanted a reminder.

prompt: A team changes ask.ts so the Android app asks at launch and, after one no, explains before asking again on the next launch. Compared with asking in context, what is still wrong?

choices.text: Explaining is forbidden on Android
choices.why: The documentation asks for it.

choices.text: Nothing; explaining fixes it
choices.why: The explanation is about a feature the student has not reached.

choices.text: Both dialogs still come before the student wants a reminder
choices.why: Right. An explanation helps, but the moment is still one where the question makes no sense.

choices.text: The rationale call returns false at launch, so it cannot explain
choices.why: After one no it returns true, at launch or anywhere.

prompt: Why does the SwiftUI fragment have no branch for a rationale?

choices.text: iOS has one dialog, so there is no second ask to explain before
choices.why: Right. Any explanation goes before the first and only ask.

choices.text: Because the purpose string in Info.plist replaces the dialog entirely
choices.why: The purpose string is part of the dialog, not a replacement for it.

choices.text: Because SwiftUI explains permissions by itself
choices.why: Nothing explains on the app's behalf.

choices.text: Because the fragment was not run
choices.why: Not running it does not change what iOS offers.

prompt: A planner update adds a photo of each course. Which approach fits this lesson best?

choices.text: Ask for full photo library access at launch, beside notifications
choices.why: Two questions with no reason in sight, at the worst moment.

choices.text: Ask when a photo is added, and work with a limited selection
choices.why: Right: in context, and accepting the partial yes.

choices.text: Skip the purpose string, since the feature is small
choices.why: On iOS the app is terminated without it.

choices.text: Ask for location too, in case photos are tagged
choices.why: A permission the feature does not need is one not to ask for.

prompt: On Android, how many times can the system dialog for one permission be shown before a refusal becomes permanent, counting both dialogs?
Which statement holds on both platforms?

choices.text: A refused permission can be asked for once more
choices.why: Only on Android, and only once.

choices.text: After the final no, only the person can turn it back on, in Settings
choices.why: Right. The app can offer the way, not take it.

choices.text: The app is told when to explain
choices.why: Only Android has that call.

choices.text: Notifications are granted at install
choices.why: Not on iOS, and not on Android 13 and later.
